title: The Clocks Changed. Our Body Clocks Did Not. | Terra
summary: We analyzed 33,000 clock changes across 107,000 people. The hour back bought 22 minutes of sleep, and three weeks on, bedtimes still hadn’t caught up.
body_markdown:
## Falling Back: Our Bodies Kept Some of Summer Time


If our bodies followed the clock perfectly, bedtimes on the clock wouldn't move at all. If they ignored it completely, people would have fallen asleep a full hour earlier on the clock. After the clocks went back last year, people fell asleep **about 9 minutes earlier** on the clock in the first week (95% interval: 7–11). Bodies took up most of the hour straight away, but not all of it. Three weeks later, bedtimes were **still about 7 minutes earlier** . We checked this the careful way: we explored part of the data first, wrote down what we expected, and then confirmed it on people we hadn't looked at.


Figure 1 shows the same picture in both directions. In the two weeks before a change, bedtimes barely moved, which also tells us the comparison works. Straight after the change, the lines split. When the clocks went back (autumn 2025), people fell asleep about 22 minutes earlier on the clock on the first night, then settled at around 5–13 minutes earlier for the rest of the three weeks. When the clocks went forward (spring 2025 and 2026), it was the reverse: about 22 minutes later on the first night, then around 10 minutes later for three weeks. Neither line made it back to zero. One more detail: on the nights just before the clocks went back, people went to bed later than usual, perhaps making the most of the hour they knew was coming. In the US, Halloween also fell on the Friday before.


Figure 1: Change in bedtime on the clock around the clock change, compared with each person's own two weeks before and with people whose clocks didn't change. About 11,800 autumn and 21,300 spring clock changes in the US and Europe, 2025–2026. Night 0 is the night of the change itself.


## Did We Get the Extra Hour of Sleep?


About a third of it, and mostly in one go. People slept **19 minutes longer** on the night the clocks went back. After that, sleep was back to normal within days. Over the whole first week, people slept **about 22 minutes more in total** . Heart rate variability and resting heart rate barely moved: changes of a fraction of a millisecond and a fraction of a beat per minute.


## It Isn't Just the Alarm Clock


On weekdays, alarms push everyone onto clock time, so we also looked at Friday and Saturday nights, when most people don't have to be up early the next morning. If the lag were only about alarms, weekend bedtimes would have snapped to the new time. However, they didn't, as two and three weeks after the change, weekend bedtimes were **8–10 minutes earlier** on the clock, about the same as on other nights. That means that our bodies lag the change. In the first week, though, the two weekend nights cancel out: on the Saturday of the change people stayed up about 10 minutes later, before their clocks went back, and the following Friday they went to bed about 8 minutes earlier.


Figure 2: How much earlier people fell asleep on the clock in the three weeks after the clocks went back in autumn 2025, on all nights and on Friday and Saturday nights only. Lines show 95% intervals. In week 1, the weekend nights include the night of the change itself. If bodies ignored the clock entirely, every bar would read −60.


## And in Spring?


Spring was the mirror image, and a bit harder. In the first week after the clocks went forward, people fell asleep **12 minutes later** on the clock (95% interval: 11–13), and still **11 minutes later** in the third week. People slept about 17 minutes less on the night of the change, and **about 22 minutes less** over the whole first week.


### Do Night Owls Pay More? A Little, Yes


The argument goes that summer time hits hardest for people whose body clock already runs late. So we grouped people by when they usually fell asleep at weekends, 2–8 weeks before the change. **Early birds** fall asleep before midnight (about three in four people). A middle group falls asleep between midnight and 1 am. **Night owls** fall asleep after 1 am: about one in ten people, typically asleep at 1:40 am and up at 9:45. Each group was compared with people of the same type whose clocks didn't change.


Across the first week after the clocks went forward, night owls lost **6.9 minutes of sleep a night** on average, against **2.9** for early birds. Three weeks on, early birds had mostly recovered (−1.2 minutes a night), while night owls were still losing about 5. In autumn, night owls also gained a little more sleep than early birds, but too little to be sure. A stricter test we had planned in advance, on people we hadn't looked at, fell just short of our bar. So we call this likely rather than certain.


Our reading: night owls probably do pay a little more, and for a little longer. That's a few minutes a night, not an hour.


Figure 3: Change in sleep per night after the clocks went forward, by usual weekend bedtime measured 2–8 weeks before the change (12,749 early-bird, 2,765 in-between and 1,750 night-owl clock changes). Lines show 95% intervals.


## So, What About Last Week?


Before the clocks went back on 25 October and 1 November, we wrote down what we expected from last year's results: bedtimes about 9 minutes earlier on the clock in the first week, and still around 7 minutes earlier three weeks on. Once three weeks of nights are in, we'll check those predictions against what actually happened and report back. If last year is a guide, the extra hour was mostly a one-night gift, and your body is still running a few minutes behind the clock.


Limitations: This is observational data, so it shows what happened around the clock changes, not why. We have no light sensor or hormone data, so we tested what the light theory predicts, not the light itself. "Bedtime" is when the wearable thinks you fell asleep, not when you went to bed. We know people's time zones but not their exact location, age or sex. The results are averages, and individual responses vary widely.
